note.en: BJJ keeps the name ashi garami for the position, the foundation of its leg lock systems, where entangling the leg is legal at advanced levels.

bannedNote.en: Prohibited in competition and free practice: judo permits joint locks on the elbow only, because the knee gives way without the graduated warning an elbow gives. Ashi-garami is preserved in katame-no-kata as formal study.

links.title: Ashi-garami on the IJF technique reference

about.en: A joint lock applied to the leg by entangling it, the classical example of why judo restricts kansetsu-waza to the elbow: knee joints give way without useful warning. Banned in competition and in randori; it survives formally in katame-no-kata, where it is studied under control.

en: Recognise it: the leg entangled and rotated rather than the arm
Competition joint locks are restricted to the elbow; leg locks are prohibited
Studied only in kata under supervision, never applied live

viNotes.en: Nothing here is practised, but the reason for the ban is worth carrying: a knee gives way without the graduated warning an elbow gives, and pressure you did not see arriving is pressure you start tapping to late. If a partner ever entangles your leg in randori and you feel load come onto the knee, tap at once rather than waiting to work out what it is.
